**(CNN) —** The European Commission handed down its ruling Wednesday in a landmark antitrust case against Intel, fining the computer chip giant a record $1.45 billion for abusing its dominant position in the central processing unit (CPU) market.

Intel plans to appeal the ruling, which could have future implications for American companies accused of “jurisdiction shopping” to avoid unfavorable antitrust verdicts. CNN’s Jim Boulden explains the fundamentals of the Intel case.

**The Commission has imposed its largest fine ever on Intel. What were its reasons?**

The European Commission says Intel abused its dominant position in the semiconductor market for years. According to the Commission, Intel systematically offered rebates to PC manufacturers and retailers to keep computers containing AMD chips off store shelves.

AMD—another American company and Intel’s only competitor—first raised concerns in 2000.

**Why does the Commission have the authority to impose such fines?**

EU law does not consider market dominance itself illegal, but it allows the Commission to fine a company that abuses its position as the largest participant in a given market. Its guidelines permit fines based on a percentage of a company’s profits.

EU law is designed to “protect consumers,” and the antitrust office says consumers were harmed. However, as Intel has emphasized, consumers did not initiate this case. AMD, a competitor, brought the complaint in Europe—as well as in Japan and South Korea—because U.S. antitrust officials under President George W. Bush were unlikely to pursue a case on these grounds.

The EU could have fined Intel—or any company—up to 10% of its global annual revenue, but it chose to base the penalty on a smaller percentage of the revenue Intel generated in the EU.

**Can Intel afford to pay the fine, and what is the company’s current position?**

Intel reported first-quarter revenue of $7 billion and can easily afford the fine. Interestingly, however, the company has lost 4% of its market share to AMD so far this year.

**Intel says it will appeal. When is the appeal likely to be heard?**

A further appeal will take months. Intel appealed a preliminary aspect of the ruling last year and lost.

Meanwhile, the European Commission could argue that Intel continues to abuse its market position and increase the fine during the appeals process, as it did in the case of Microsoft.

**Intel is not the first technology company to be penalized by the European Commission. What about Microsoft?**

The antitrust unit has launched another round of investigations into Microsoft. The company has already paid its fine, and the EU continues to monitor its conduct in connection with the earlier matters.

**What kind of precedent does the Intel case set?**

The EU has fined many cartels and companies found to have abused their market positions. However, it rarely imposes penalties on major American companies based on complaints filed by American competitors. The case therefore attracts particular attention, especially among critics who accuse American companies of “jurisdiction shopping” to secure favorable outcomes.

**(CNN) —** On Wednesday, the European Commission concluded a major antitrust case against Intel by imposing a record $1.45 billion penalty. The chipmaker was found to have misused its leading position in the market for computer processing units, or CPUs. Intel intends to appeal the decision.

CNN’s Jim Boulden outlines the case, which could affect how similar complaints against U.S. companies are handled in the future. It has also drawn attention from critics who claim some American businesses engage in “jurisdiction shopping” to avoid unfavorable antitrust judgments.

**Why did the European Commission impose its largest-ever fine?**

According to the Commission, Intel spent years exploiting its dominance in the semiconductor industry. Regulators allege that the company repeatedly offered rebates to computer manufacturers and retailers on the condition that systems using chips made by AMD were kept out of stores.

AMD—also a U.S. company and Intel’s sole competitor—first raised concerns in 2000.

**What gives the Commission authority to issue a penalty of this size?**

European Union law does not prohibit a company from holding a dominant market position. It does, however, allow regulators to punish a business that takes advantage of its status as the largest participant in a particular market.

The EU uses guidelines that calculate fines as a percentage of a company’s profits. Its legal framework is intended to protect consumers, and the antitrust office maintains that Intel’s conduct caused consumer harm.

Intel counters that consumers did not initiate the complaint. Instead, AMD pursued cases in Europe, Japan, and South Korea, at a time when U.S. antitrust authorities under President George W. Bush were considered unlikely to act on such grounds.

The EU had the authority to penalize Intel—or any other company—by as much as 10% of its worldwide annual revenue. In this case, however, it chose a lower percentage based on revenue generated within the EU.

**Is Intel financially capable of paying the fine, and how is the company performing?**

Intel recorded $7 billion in revenue during the first quarter, meaning it can comfortably cover the penalty. At the same time, it has lost four percentage points of market share to AMD so far this year.

**When could Intel’s appeal be considered?**

A further appeal is expected to take months. Intel challenged an initial portion of the decision the previous year but was unsuccessful.

While the appeal is underway, the Commission may argue that Intel’s abusive conduct is continuing and could raise the penalty. It previously took that approach with Microsoft.

**Has the European Commission also acted against Microsoft?**

Yes. The EU’s antitrust division has opened another series of investigations into Microsoft. The company has already paid its earlier fine, and European regulators continue to monitor its behavior in connection with the previous issues.

**What precedent might the Intel ruling establish?**

European authorities have penalized many cartels and companies accused of abusing market power. However, it is unusual for the EU to fine a major American corporation following a complaint from another U.S. company. That makes the Intel case especially notable, particularly among those who say American businesses seek out favorable legal jurisdictions to secure more advantageous results.

# Intel’s $1.45 billion EU antitrust fine, explained

**Brussels** — The European Commission imposed a record **€1.06 billion, then about $1.45 billion, fine on Intel in May 2009**, saying the US chipmaker illegally used its dominance to shut rival Advanced Micro Devices out of the market.

Here’s what the ruling meant.

## Why was Intel fined?

EU regulators concluded that Intel abused its dominant position in the market for **x86 central processing units**, the chips used in most personal computers.

The Commission said that between 2002 and 2007 Intel:

- Offered rebates to computer makers including Dell, HP, NEC and Lenovo on the condition that they bought all, or nearly all, of their x86 processors from Intel.
- Paid retailer Media-Saturn to sell computers containing Intel chips while excluding machines powered by AMD processors.
- Made payments intended to delay or restrict the launch of certain AMD-based computers.

Discounts themselves are not illegal. The Commission’s case was that Intel’s rebates and payments were conditional and designed to prevent an efficient competitor from reaching customers.

Intel denied that it had harmed competition, arguing that the market remained highly competitive and that its discounts benefited consumers.

## How can the EU fine an American company?

The European Union can enforce its competition laws against any company doing business in the European Economic Area, regardless of where that company is headquartered.

At the time, the case was brought under **Article 82 of the European Community Treaty**, now Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. That provision prohibits dominant companies from abusing their market power.

The Commission can fine a company as much as **10% of its worldwide annual revenue**. The key question is not whether the company is European, but whether its conduct affects competition and consumers in Europe.

## Could Intel afford the penalty?

Yes. Although the fine was unprecedented for a single EU antitrust case, it was well below the maximum permitted under European law.

Intel reported roughly **$37.6 billion in revenue for 2008**, meaning the $1.45 billion penalty represented less than 4% of one year’s sales. The company also had substantial cash and investments.

That did not make the penalty insignificant. It reduced earnings and created potential consequences for Intel’s relationships with customers, but it did not threaten the company’s survival.

## What did Intel plan to do?

Intel said it would appeal, contending that the Commission had misunderstood both its rebates and the competitive state of the chip market.

An appeal would go first to the EU’s General Court and potentially to the European Court of Justice. Such litigation can take years. Filing an appeal does not automatically erase the fine; companies generally must pay it or provide an acceptable financial guarantee while the case is reviewed.

## How did the fine compare with Microsoft’s?

Before the Intel decision, Microsoft had been the most prominent American target of European antitrust enforcement.

In 2004, the Commission fined Microsoft **€497 million** for abusing its dominance in personal-computer operating systems. It later imposed additional penalties, including an **€899 million fine in 2008**, for failing to comply with parts of the earlier ruling.

Intel’s **€1.06 billion** penalty was larger than Microsoft’s original antitrust fine and was described as the biggest single antitrust fine the Commission had imposed on one company at that time. The Microsoft penalties, however, collectively amounted to more.

The cases also involved different conduct. Microsoft’s centered on interoperability information and the bundling of software, while Intel’s focused on rebates and payments allegedly used to exclude a rival chipmaker.

## What did it mean for other American companies?

The ruling reinforced a principle already demonstrated by the Microsoft cases: **US companies operating internationally must comply with EU competition rules even when their conduct is lawful—or treated differently—at home.**

It did not create a special rule for American businesses. European and non-European companies are subject to the same legal standards. But the size of the fine signaled that Brussels was prepared to use its authority aggressively against major global corporations.

For dominant companies, the practical warning was clear: rebates, exclusivity arrangements and customer incentives can attract EU scrutiny if regulators believe they are structured to block competitors rather than compete on price or quality.

counterfactuals.output:
### What was the Intel–EU antitrust case?

The European Commission accused Intel of abusing its dominant position in the market for x86 computer processors to impede its principal rival, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). In May 2009, the Commission found that Intel had violated EU competition law.

### What role did AMD’s complaint play?

AMD filed a complaint with the European Commission in 2000, alleging that Intel used its market power and commercial arrangements with computer manufacturers to exclude AMD processors. The complaint helped trigger a lengthy investigation involving manufacturers, retailers, and Intel’s internal business practices.

### What rebate practices were alleged?

The Commission said Intel gave rebates to major computer makers—including Dell, HP, NEC, and Lenovo—on the condition that they buy all or nearly all of their x86 processors from Intel. It also alleged that Intel paid retailer Media-Saturn to sell only computers containing Intel chips.

According to the Commission, these were not ordinary volume discounts. They were “conditional” or “exclusivity” rebates capable of making it economically difficult for customers to switch even part of their purchases to AMD.

### Were there other allegations?

Yes. The Commission said Intel made payments to manufacturers to delay, cancel, or limit the distribution of certain computers using AMD processors. These practices were sometimes described as “naked restrictions,” because they directly discouraged particular AMD-based products rather than operating through a general rebate program.

### How large was the fine?

The Commission imposed a **€1.06 billion** fine—about **$1.45 billion at the time**. It was then the largest antitrust fine imposed by the EU on a single company.

### Could Intel appeal?

Yes. EU competition decisions can be challenged first before the EU’s General Court and then, on points of law, before the Court of Justice of the European Union.

Intel pursued those appeals. After several rounds of litigation, the General Court in 2022 annulled the part of the decision concerning the rebates and set aside the original €1.06 billion fine, finding that the Commission’s economic analysis was insufficient. The EU’s highest court upheld that result in 2024.

The “naked restrictions” findings remained. In 2023, the Commission imposed a new **€376.36 million** fine for that conduct, which Intel also challenged.

### Why was the case important for U.S. technology firms?

The case demonstrated that U.S. companies operating in Europe are fully subject to EU competition law, even when the companies and much of the relevant technology originate in the United States. It also showed that:

- dominant firms must be careful with loyalty or exclusivity rebates;
- European regulators may scrutinize conduct more aggressively than U.S. authorities;
- global pricing and distribution practices can create liability in multiple jurisdictions;
- EU fines can be extremely large; and
- regulators must still prove that challenged practices are capable of restricting competition, particularly when a company submits detailed economic evidence.

More broadly, the case became a major precedent in the debate over whether antitrust enforcement should focus on the formal structure of rebates or on their demonstrated ability to exclude an equally efficient competitor.

**Wednesday**

**BRUSSELS —** The European Commission’s decision Wednesday to fine Intel a record $1.45 billion for abusing its dominance of the computer-chip market marks the latest clash between U.S. technology companies and European regulators — and is likely to renew debate over “jurisdiction shopping” in global antitrust cases.

The commission said Intel used rebates and other incentives to discourage computer manufacturers and retailers from using chips made by rival Advanced Micro Devices. Regulators ordered Intel to end the practices and imposed a €1.06 billion penalty, worth about $1.45 billion at the time.

Intel denied wrongdoing and said it would appeal, arguing that its discounts reflected aggressive but lawful competition in the market for x86 central processing units, or CPUs. The company has long maintained that consumers benefited from falling prices, improved performance and rapid innovation.

European Competition Commissioner Neelie Kroes said Intel had harmed competition by using its market power to shut out a rival rather than competing solely on the merits of its products.

The ruling highlights Europe’s increasingly prominent role in policing multinational companies. Because technology markets cross national borders, conduct involving the same companies can be examined by regulators in several countries. That gives complainants opportunities to seek out the jurisdiction most likely to pursue a case — a practice critics sometimes call jurisdiction shopping.

From one perspective, jurisdiction shopping allows a company that believes it has been unfairly excluded from a market to seek relief when regulators elsewhere decline to act. European authorities also argue that they have an obligation to protect consumers and competition within the 27-nation bloc, regardless of where a company is headquartered.

But the practice can create friction. A business cleared — or subjected to a limited remedy — in one country may still face a major penalty in another. Different legal standards can also produce conflicting conclusions about whether rebates represent legitimate price competition or an unlawful effort to exclude rivals.

The Intel case follows a series of major European actions against U.S. technology companies, including Microsoft. Those cases have fueled complaints that Brussels applies antitrust law more aggressively than Washington, particularly when dealing with dominant American firms.

Supporters of the European approach say that characterization overlooks the global reach of the companies involved and the economic importance of the European market. They contend that without multiple enforcement centers, dominant firms could benefit from gaps or differences in national regulation.

The broader issue is unlikely to disappear. As markets become more international, companies can expect decisions made in one region to be scrutinized in several others. For regulators, the challenge will be distinguishing legitimate cross-border enforcement from duplicative investigations or attempts to find the most favorable legal venue.

Intel’s appeal could take years. In the meantime, Wednesday’s decision sends a clear message: Winning in the marketplace does not shield a global company from scrutiny in every jurisdiction where it does business.

Produce an accessible FAQ addressing whether Intel can afford the penalty, why EU regulators have jurisdiction, and how the case compares with Microsoft’s antitrust troubles.
counterfactuals.output:
## Intel antitrust fine: an accessible FAQ

### What did the European Commission do?

On 13 May 2009, the Commission fined Intel **€1.06 billion**—about **$1.45 billion at the time**. It was then the largest single EU antitrust fine imposed on one company.

The Commission concluded that Intel had abused its dominant position in the market for **x86 computer processors**, chiefly to obstruct its smaller rival AMD.

### What exactly was Intel accused of?

The Commission said that between 2002 and 2007 Intel used two principal tactics:

- **Conditional rebates:** Intel gave major computer manufacturers—including Dell, HP, NEC and Lenovo—rebates if they bought all, or nearly all, of their x86 processors from Intel.
- **Payments for exclusion or delay:** It allegedly paid manufacturers to postpone, cancel or restrict products using AMD chips, and paid retailer Media-Saturn to sell only computers containing Intel processors.

Discounts are not automatically unlawful. The Commission’s objection was that these arrangements were tied to exclusivity and could prevent an equally efficient competitor from gaining access to customers.

### Why was the fine so large?

EU fines reflect factors including:

- the seriousness of the infringement;
- how long it lasted;
- the size of the affected market;
- the company’s sales; and
- the need for deterrence.

The penalty represented roughly **4.15% of Intel’s 2008 annual turnover**, below the legal maximum of 10%.

### Was Intel being punished simply for being dominant?

No. EU law does not prohibit a company from becoming dominant through better products or efficiency. But a dominant company has a “special responsibility” not to use practices that improperly shut competitors out of the market.

The Commission’s case was about Intel’s alleged conduct, not its large market share by itself.

### Could Intel afford the penalty?

Yes. The fine was substantial but did not threaten Intel’s survival.

Intel reported approximately **$37.6 billion in 2008 revenue** and **$5.3 billion in net income**, and it held billions in cash and liquid investments. The fine was therefore financially manageable, although large enough to affect earnings and attract shareholder attention.

### Why did EU regulators have jurisdiction over an American company?

EU competition law applies to business conduct that is carried out in, or has substantial effects within, the European Economic Area. It does not matter where the company is incorporated.

Intel sold processors throughout Europe, and the disputed arrangements involved computers and retailers serving European consumers. That gave the Commission jurisdiction under what was then **Article 82 of the EC Treaty**, now **Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union**.

This is similar to the way US antitrust authorities may investigate foreign companies whose conduct affects American commerce.

### Didn’t US regulators have authority too?

Yes. US and EU authorities can examine the same conduct under their own laws. Their legal tests and remedies, however, are not identical.

At the time of the EU decision, Intel was also facing antitrust scrutiny and private litigation elsewhere. The US Federal Trade Commission later brought its own case, which Intel settled in 2010 without admitting liability.

### How did this compare with Microsoft’s EU antitrust troubles?

There were important similarities:

- Both were large US technology companies considered dominant in important markets.
- Both were accused of using that dominance to disadvantage rivals.
- Both challenged the Commission’s reasoning and penalties in the EU courts.
- In neither case was dominance itself illegal.

But the conduct differed:

- **Microsoft’s case** centered principally on withholding interoperability information and tying Windows Media Player to Windows.
- **Intel’s case** centered on rebates, exclusivity arrangements and payments allegedly designed to limit the sale of AMD-based computers.

In 2004 Microsoft received a **€497 million** fine, followed by further penalties for failing to comply with the Commission’s order. Microsoft’s accumulated EU penalties eventually exceeded Intel’s original fine, but Intel’s €1.06 billion sanction was, when announced, the **largest single antitrust fine against one company**.

### What was supposed to happen after the 2009 decision?

Intel was ordered to stop the unlawful practices and appealed to the EU’s General Court. An appeal did not automatically suspend the decision: Intel generally had to pay the fine or provide a bank guarantee while litigation continued.

EU antitrust appeals can take years. Courts review whether the Commission proved the infringement, followed proper procedures and calculated the penalty lawfully.

### Did Intel ultimately win?

On the original €1.06 billion penalty, substantially yes—but only after a very long legal battle.

- **2014:** The General Court upheld the Commission’s decision.
- **2017:** The EU Court of Justice set that judgment aside, saying the lower court needed to examine more carefully whether Intel’s rebates were actually capable of excluding an equally efficient competitor.
- **2022:** The General Court annulled the part of the decision concerning the rebates and cancelled the entire €1.06 billion fine because the court could not determine what portion related to the remaining conduct.
- **2024:** The Court of Justice rejected the Commission’s appeal, leaving that outcome in place.

### Does that mean the whole case disappeared?

No. The courts did not erase every Commission finding. Certain “naked restrictions”—payments allegedly made to manufacturers to delay, cancel or limit AMD-based products—remained legally distinct from the rebate findings.

In 2023 the Commission imposed a new, smaller fine of **€376.36 million** for those restrictions. Intel challenged that decision as well. Thus, the record-setting 2009 fine was annulled, but litigation arising from the underlying conduct continued.

### What is the broader significance?

The case became a major test of how EU law should assess loyalty rebates by dominant companies. It pushed regulators and courts toward a more effects-based inquiry: not merely asking whether a rebate was conditional, but examining whether it was realistically capable of excluding a competitor that was as efficient as the dominant firm.

# EU hits Intel with record $1.45 billion antitrust fine

**By CNN Business staff, with analysis from Jim Boulden**  
**BRUSSELS, Belgium — May 13, 2009**

European regulators imposed a record €1.06 billion ($1.45 billion) fine on Intel Wednesday, ruling that the U.S. chipmaker abused its dominant position to shut rival Advanced Micro Devices out of the market.

The European Commission said Intel used rebates and payments to persuade major computer manufacturers to buy all, or nearly all, of their x86 processors from Intel. Regulators also accused the company of paying a leading European electronics retailer to stock only computers powered by Intel chips.

Intel denied that it broke the law and said it would appeal.

The decision is one of the European Union’s most significant competition cases against a U.S. technology company. It could shape how regulators assess loyalty rebates and other incentives offered by dominant businesses.

## The rebate allegations

The commission said Intel granted conditional rebates to Dell, Hewlett-Packard, NEC and Lenovo in return for buying most or all of their processors from Intel.

It also alleged that Intel made payments to computer makers to delay, cancel or restrict products using chips from AMD, its much smaller competitor.

In the retail market, regulators said Intel paid Germany’s Media-Saturn, owner of the Media Markt chain, on the condition that its stores sell only computers containing Intel processors.

Such arrangements may have reduced prices for the companies receiving the incentives, but the commission argued that their broader effect was to make it harder for AMD to reach consumers.

EU Competition Commissioner Neelie Kroes described Intel’s conduct as a sustained effort to exclude its only major rival from the market. The practices identified by the commission ran mainly from 2002 to 2007.

Intel said its rebates were legitimate discounts based on sales volumes and that competition in the processor market remained intense.

## AMD’s role

AMD helped trigger the investigation by filing a complaint with European regulators in 2000. The company has long alleged that Intel used its market power and relationships with computer manufacturers to limit AMD’s access to store shelves and major supply contracts.

The case therefore focused not simply on which company produced the better or cheaper chip, but on whether computer makers had a genuine commercial opportunity to use AMD processors.

AMD welcomed the ruling, saying it would help create a more open market. Intel countered that AMD’s gains and losses reflected product performance and business decisions rather than unlawful exclusion.

## What EU law prohibits

European competition law does not make it illegal for a company to be large or dominant. But Article 82 of the European Community Treaty — now Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union — prohibits a dominant company from abusing that position in ways that restrict competition.

The commission concluded that Intel held a dominant share of the market for x86 central processing units, the chips that power most personal computers.

Conditional rebates can be unlawful when they are designed to tie customers to a dominant supplier and deny rivals enough access to compete. The EU’s case was that Intel’s incentives formed part of a wider exclusionary strategy, rather than ordinary price competition.

## A high-stakes appeal

Intel can challenge the decision before the EU’s General Court and, on points of law, before the European Court of Justice.

CNN’s Jim Boulden said the size of the fine would draw headlines, but the more important battle would concern the commission’s reasoning. Intel is likely to argue that regulators treated commercially normal rebates as anticompetitive without showing sufficient harm to consumers.

The company could also challenge how the commission calculated the fine and whether the evidence proved that its arrangements were capable of excluding an equally efficient competitor.

But appeals of EU competition decisions are difficult. Courts generally examine whether the commission followed proper procedures, supported its conclusions with evidence and applied the law correctly; they do not simply rehear the case from the beginning.

“Intel has every reason to fight,” Boulden’s analysis noted, “because the consequences go well beyond the immediate financial penalty. The ruling affects how the company negotiates with manufacturers and how dominant technology businesses structure discounts.”

## A precedent beyond computer chips

The decision could become a benchmark for other industries in which a dominant supplier offers rebates based on exclusivity or on a customer purchasing nearly all its requirements from one company.

A final judgment upholding the commission’s approach would strengthen Brussels’ ability to scrutinize loyalty discounts even when they reduce a buyer’s short-term costs. It would also signal that behind-the-scenes contracts with manufacturers and retailers can attract the same attention as pricing aimed directly at consumers.

For technology companies, the broader message is that competition authorities may examine not only what a product costs, but also whether a rival can realistically get its product into factories, stores and customers’ hands.

The fine represented roughly 4% of Intel’s 2008 revenue and was the largest penalty the commission had imposed on a single company at the time. Yet the lasting importance of the case may be measured less by the amount Intel must pay than by the rules it establishes for dominant companies across Europe.
